title: Connection pool exhaustion causes cascading API failures
description: Diagnose and fix database connection pool exhaustion that triggers cascading API failures under load, using connection leak detection, pool sizing, and circuit breakers.

data.text: During a flash sale, your API starts returning 500 and 503 errors across multiple endpoints. CPU and memory are fine, but database connection pool metrics show 100% utilization with a growing queue of waiting requests. A single slow query on a reporting endpoint is holding connections, starving the rest of the application.

items: Database connection pool utilization hits 100% and stays there
New requests wait in a connection queue until they timeout (typically 15-30 seconds)
Healthy endpoints start returning 503 because they cannot get a connection in time
Application logs show 'Timeout expired' or 'Connection pool full' errors
The database CPU remains low because connections are waiting, not querying
Thread dump reveals many threads blocked on connection acquisition

terms.definition: A cache of database connections maintained so they can be reused when future requests to the database are required.
A connection that is opened but never returned to the pool, often due to missing Dispose() or unclosed using blocks.
A failure in one component that causes failures in dependent components, propagating through the system.
Isolating resources such as connection pools so that one failing endpoint cannot consume all connections.
A pattern that stops sending requests to a failing service after a threshold, giving it time to recover.

items: A long-running query holds connections for seconds while the pool is sized for millisecond operations
Connection leaks in a new code path that does not properly dispose DbContext or IDbConnection
Pool size was never tuned for the application's concurrency requirements
A retry policy retries failed queries, multiplying the number of open connections
Multiple microservices share the same database user and connection pool limits

cards.title: Default pool size
cards.description: Use the framework default (e.g., 100 for .NET, 20 for Npgsql).

cards.title: Formula-based sizing
cards.description: Calculate based on cores, latency, and concurrency: (cores * 2) + spindles.

cards.title: Bulkhead pools
cards.description: Separate pools for critical and non-critical operations.

cards.title: Connection multiplexing
cards.description: Use a proxy like PgBouncer to pool connections at the infrastructure layer.

data.title: Connection leak from missing dispose
data.content: A DbContext is created but never disposed, leaking connections:

data.caption: Connection pool exhaustion leading to cascading failures
data.definition:
graph TD
    A[Flash sale traffic spike] --> B[More requests need DB connections]
    B --> C[Slow query holds connection for 5s]
    C --> D[Pool utilization reaches 100%]
    D --> E[New requests queue for connection]
    E --> F[Request timeout after 15s]
    F --> G[503 returned to client]
    G --> H[Healthy endpoints also timeout]
    H --> I[Cascading API failures]

data.title: Pool size is not the only knob
data.text: Increasing the pool size without fixing the underlying leak or slow query only delays the failure. Address connection lifecycle and query performance first, then tune the pool.

data.title: Detect and fix a connection leak
data.description: Use a profiling tool or APM to find connection leaks in an application. Fix the leak and document the root cause.
steps: Enable connection pool performance counters or APM connection tracking
Identify endpoints with the highest connection acquisition time
Search the codebase for DbContext or IDbConnection instances without using statements
Fix each leak by adding proper disposal
Verify pool utilization returns to normal under the same load
data.expectedOutcome: You should see connection pool metrics return to healthy levels and a reduction in timeout errors under load.

data.title: Summary
points: Monitor connection pool utilization, queue length, and acquisition time
Fix connection leaks before increasing pool size
Use bulkhead pools to protect critical endpoints from noisy neighbors
Add circuit breakers so timeouts do not cascade into full outages
data.takeaway: Connection pool exhaustion is a reliability problem, not just a performance problem. It turns one slow query into a system-wide outage.
